en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Non-Proliferation, Concerning the Question on Inference.
1. The Question on Non-Proliferation “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, dwell delighting in non-proliferation, taking delight in non-proliferation. What, then, is that non-proliferation?”

“The fruit of stream-entry, Great King, is free from conceptual proliferation; the fruit of once-returning is free from conceptual proliferation; the fruit of non-returning is free from conceptual proliferation; the fruit of arhatship is free from conceptual proliferation.

“If, venerable Nāgasena, the fruit of stream-entry is free from conceptual proliferation, and the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are free from conceptual proliferation, for what purpose then do these bhikkhus recite and inquire about the discourses, the mixed prose and verse, and the systematic expositions?”

“The Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—do they not get entangled in these through building work, giving, and worship? Are they not performing actions that have been rejected by the Conqueror?
“Those monks, O Great King, who recite and inquire about the Sutta, Geyya, Vyākaraṇa, and Gāthā...”
The Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—these are hindered by new undertakings, by giving, and by worship;
yet all of them perform these acts for the attainment of the state beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Those, O Great King, who are pure by nature and whose latent tendencies have been cultivated in the past, become free from conceptual proliferation in a single moment of consciousness.
But those monks who possess great defilements become free from conceptual proliferation (*nippapañca*) through these methods.
Great King, it is just as if one man, having sown seed in a field, were to harvest the grain by his own strength and effort alone, without a fence or a wall;
while another man, having sown seed in a field, enters the forest and [gathers] wood and branches...
Having cut down the fence and wall, one might harvest the grain. That search for the fence and wall there was for the sake of the grain.

Even so, Great King, those who are by nature pure and have been perfumed by past habituation become free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) in a single moment of consciousness, like a person harvesting grain without a fence or wall.

But those monks who possess great defilement (*mahārajakkha*) become free from conceptual proliferation (*nippapañca*) through these methods, like a man who has cleared away grain after building a fence and wall.
Or again, Great King, it is as if there were a cluster of fruit at the very top of a vast mango tree;
then, if anyone possessing supernormal power (*iddhimā*) were to come there and take that fruit, whereas one who lacks such power—
Having cut wood and creepers and bound them into a ladder, he would climb that tree by means of it and gather the fruit.
Whatever search for a ladder he undertakes there is for the sake of the fruit.

In the same way, Great King, those who are naturally pure and have been perfumed by past habituation become free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) in a single moment of consciousness, like one possessing psychic power gathering the fruit of a tree.
But those bhikkhus who possess great defilements realize the Truths by means of this method, just as a man might gather fruit from a tree using a ladder.
Or again, Great King, it is like a certain litigant who, being alone, approaches his master and settles the case;
whereas another wealthy man, having increased his following by means of his wealth, settles the case through that assembly.
The search for an assembly there is for the sake of a purpose.

In the same way, Great King, those who are naturally pure and have previously cultivated their mental impressions attain mastery over the six higher knowledges in a single moment of consciousness, like a man acting alone to accomplish his purpose.
But those bhikkhus who possess great defilements accomplish the goal of recluseship through these various means, like a man accomplishing his purpose with an assembly.
"Recitation, Great King, is very helpful; inquiry is very helpful; new construction is very helpful; giving is very helpful; and worship is very helpful for those various tasks.

Just as, Great King, a man who serves a king and has performed his duties [is assisted] by ministers, soldiers, troops, gatekeepers, commanders, and courtiers—all of them become helpers to him when his business arises."

In the same way, Great King, the recitation of the texts is very helpful, inquiry is very helpful, new construction work is very helpful, giving is very helpful, and worship is very helpful for those various duties.
If, Great King, all beings were pure by birth alone, there would be no need for instruction.
But because, Great King, there is a need for hearing [the Dhamma], the Elder Sāriputta, Great King, [has practiced] for immeasurable, incalculable eons.
"Even one who has accumulated roots of merit and reached the pinnacle of wisdom was unable to attain the destruction of the taints without hearing [the Dhamma].
Therefore, Great King, hearing is of great benefit; likewise are recitation and interrogation.
Thus, even recitation and interrogation are unproliferated and conditioned."
“Venerable Nāgasena, the question has been well-explained; it is so, and thus do I accept it.
This is the first question on the absence of conceptual proliferation (nippapañca).
